questions.question: What is an edge effect in a habitat?
choices: A change found equally throughout every habitat
A process that occurs only at the center of a forest
A guarantee that all boundary areas support identical species
A difference in conditions near a habitat boundary compared with its interior

questions.question: What is a wildlife corridor?
choices: A connection that can allow organisms to move between habitat patches
A wall that prevents all animal movement
A site designed only for waste disposal
A road with no ecological function

questions.question: What is ecological restoration?
choices: Replacing diverse communities with one uniform crop
Assisting recovery of a degraded ecosystem
Keeping every species at an unchanging number forever
Moving degraded material elsewhere without assisting recovery

questions.question: What is a reference ecosystem used for in restoration?
choices: A guarantee that all restored sites become identical
A replacement for measuring the restored site's progress
A comparison that helps define recovery goals
A rule that local conditions can be ignored

questions.question: What is an invasive species?
choices: Every nonnative species regardless of effects
Every native species with rapid growth
Any organism moving between two habitat patches
A nonnative species whose establishment causes or is likely to cause harm

questions.question: What is a riparian zone?
choices: Land alongside a river or stream
The open water at the center of a lake
The deep ocean floor below coastal water
Land defined only by permanent desert conditions

questions.question: What is ecological succession?
choices: Movement of one animal for one afternoon
Change in community composition over time
Permanent stability of every species
The loss of every nutrient from soil

questions.question: Why can fragmentation reduce gene flow between populations?
choices: Patch separation always increases movement between them
Gene flow does not depend on movement or reproduction
Separated patches can limit movement and mating
Every patch necessarily keeps the same allele frequencies forever

questions.question: How can restoring native plants benefit some local animals?
choices: Every native plant supports every animal equally
Native plants never compete for soil resources
Native plants eliminate all disease in local animals
They can supply suitable food and habitat relationships

questions.question: Why is removing a stressor often important before planting for restoration?
choices: Ongoing disturbance can prevent newly planted communities from establishing
Planting guarantees recovery despite unchanged disturbance
Removing a stressor replaces the need to set any goal
Stressors affect only mature plants and never seedlings

questions.question: How can vegetation along a stream reduce sediment entering the water?
choices: Roots guarantee that no sediment moves during any flood
Roots stabilize soil and vegetation slows runoff
Vegetation increases erosion in every soil condition
Plants stop rainfall before it reaches the stream

questions.question: Why monitor a restored site over several years?
choices: One photograph proves permanent recovery
Recovery has no time-dependent changes
Recovery and unintended effects can change over time
Monitoring alone guarantees every goal is reached

questions.question: Why may reintroducing a species fail if habitat conditions remain unsuitable?
choices: Reintroduction removes every food and shelter requirement
All species tolerate any temperature and water conditions
A released population survives regardless of habitat quality
The original limits on survival may still exist

questions.question: How can a wildlife crossing help where a road divides habitat?
choices: It can reduce barriers and dangerous crossings
It guarantees that no animal is ever harmed by traffic
It prevents every form of habitat fragmentation
It makes all species use exactly the same route

questions.question: Why can restoration involve tradeoffs rather than one perfect outcome?
choices: Every ecosystem has identical recovery needs
Goals, species needs, resources, and site conditions can conflict
All goals can always be met with no resource limits
Only one species uses any habitat

questions.question: After wetland drainage, a project restores more natural water flow. Which restoration element is directly addressed?
choices: Atomic number
Stellar brightness
Hydrology
Magnetic polarity

questions.question: A restored site has more plants but only one species. Which measurement would add useful information about recovery?
choices: Only the total number of plants, counted again
Only the cost of the original planting
Only the project's area without any ecological observations
Native species diversity and community structure

questions.question: Two habitat patches reconnect, and individuals move between them. Which outcome becomes more possible?
choices: Gene flow between the populations
Immediate elimination of all variation
Permanent isolation of both populations
Complete prevention of reproduction

questions.question: A restoration treatment increases plant survival, but an untreated comparison also improves equally. What conclusion is warranted?
choices: The treatment alone must explain both improvements
The data do not isolate a benefit of the treatment
The comparison site has no scientific value
All monitoring should stop immediately

questions.question: An invasive plant returns after initial removal. What does this suggest for management?
choices: One removal guarantees permanent control
The returning plant automatically becomes native
Follow-up monitoring and repeated control may be needed
Recovery cannot be measured after any species returns
